query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the degree of atomic size mismatch, which creates local lattice distortions that act as kinetic barriers to elemental diffusion and segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles fabricated by physical or chemical approaches.
generation.intervention: Design two sets of nanoparticles with comparable overall compositions but systematically varied by choosing element combinations with high versus low atomic size mismatch.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment under catalytic conditions (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K) in controlled atmospheres (both inert and reactive) for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions induced by the atomic size mismatch among constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Large atomic size mismatches lead to enhanced lattice strain, which slows down atomic diffusion and suppresses segregation or phase separation, thus preserving the near-equiatomic solid-solution structure at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered with higher atomic size mismatch will exhibit reduced segregation and maintain a more uniform elemental distribution over time under the test conditions compared to nanoparticles with minimal size mismatch.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with little atomic size mismatch are expected to undergo more rapid elemental segregation and phase transformation under the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to operate within the specified temperature ranges for catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications and may be most pronounced in nanoparticles where surface energy effects do not dominate over the bulk stabilizing entropy contributions.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how other factors—such as synthesis-induced defects, variations in surface energy, or reactive atmospheres—might interplay with the atomic size mismatch effect under actual service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles with the same overall composition but different atomic size mismatches. Subject both sets to identical thermal treatments under inert and reactive atmospheres at the relevant temperatures (e.g., 773 K for catalytic conditions and 473 K for thermoelectric conditions). After predefined exposure times, use high-resolution electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to assess the degree of elemental segregation and phase changes.
measurements: Elemental mapping via atom probe tomography or EDS
Phase identification using X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with higher atomic size mismatch do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in structural and chemical stability (i.e., reduced segregation or phase transformation) compared to the low-size-mismatch group, then the hypothesis is falsified.
